hook: A function turns inputs into outputs. Often you know the output and need the input: what time gave this temperature, what angle has this sine. That is the job of an inverse function. In Unit 3 you will find how fast an inverse changes, using one fact you can see in a picture: reflecting a graph across $y = x$ flips its slopes.

prereq.q: If $f(x) = x^2$ and $g(x) = x + 1$, what is $f(g(x))$?

figure.caption: $f$ and $f^{-1}$ are mirror images across $y = x$. The point $(1, 3)$ on $f$ becomes $(3, 1)$ on $f^{-1}$, and the slope 2 there becomes $\frac{1}{2}$.

chain.cause: $f$ sends each input $a$ to an output $b$, and no two inputs share an output (one-to-one)
chain.effect: the inverse function $f^{-1}$ sends $b$ back to $a$: $f^{-1}(b) = a$ exactly when $f(a) = b$
swaps the coordinates of every point, reflecting the graph across $y = x$

chain.cause: Swapping coordinates swaps rise and run
chain.effect: slopes at matching points are reciprocals

chain.cause: Sine, cosine and tangent repeat, so they are not one-to-one
chain.effect: their inverses use restricted ranges: arcsine and arctangent give angles from −π/2 to π/2, arccosine from 0 to π

ideas: $f^{-1}(b) = a$ means $f(a) = b$. So $f(f^{-1}(x)) = x$ and $f^{-1}(f(x)) = x$ on the right domains.
Only a one-to-one function (each output from one input; passes the horizontal line test) has an inverse. Restrict the domain if needed.
To find a formula: write $x = f(y)$ and solve for $y$.
$\arcsin x$ and $\arctan x$ return angles in $\left[-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]$; $\arccos x$ returns angles in $[0, \pi]$.

misconception.right: $f^{-1}$ undoes $f$: if $f(2) = 7$ then $f^{-1}(7) = 2$. The reciprocal $\frac{1}{f(x)}$ is a different function. $\sin^{-1} x$ is $\arcsin x$; $\frac{1}{\sin x}$ is $\csc x$.

summary: An inverse function runs a one-to-one function backward: $f^{-1}(b) = a$ exactly when $f(a) = b$. Its graph is the reflection of $f$ across $y = x$, so points swap coordinates and slopes become reciprocals. Find a formula by solving $x = f(y)$ for $y$. The inverse trig functions use restricted ranges, and $f^{-1}$ never means $\frac{1}{f}$.
